nutshell: Biometric recognition (face, gait, person ReID) is normally trained and evaluated in a closed-set way, but real deployments are open-set - some probes have no match in the gallery. Standard losses (softmax, triplet) treat genuine and imposter scores symmetrically and ignore that open-set thresholds are set by the largest imposter scores, so the paper proposes two new losses - an Identification-Detection loss and a Relative Threshold Minimization loss - trained on simulated open-set mini-batches, applicable to any biometric modality without changing the backbone architecture.
contributions: Identification-Detection loss (L^IDL): a differentiable product of a detection score (sigmoid around a threshold sampled from in-batch non-mated scores) and an identification score (based on a differentiable softrank), trained on mini-batches that simulate open-set gallery/probe/mated/non-mated splits.

Relative Threshold Minimization (RTM) loss: minimizes a softmax-weighted average of non-mated-probe-to-gallery similarity scores, which adaptively pushes down the highest-ranking imposter scores (the ones that actually set the open-set threshold) more than lower ones - shown empirically to beat a hard-max version of the same idea.

A from-scratch open-set evaluation protocol for gait and person ReID (which lack official open-set splits): 50 random resamplings of non-mated probes at a fixed 21.5% non-mated rate, reporting median FNIR@FPIR for stability.

Demonstrated as a drop-in loss addition (no architecture change) across three modalities - face (AdaFace), gait (GaitBase, SwinGait-3D), person ReID (CAL) - improving both open-set (FNIR@FPIR) and closed-set (Rank-1) metrics simultaneously, at negligible extra training FLOPs and zero extra inference cost (Table 6).
deficiencies: The narrative text states the person-ReID result as 'a rank-1 accuracy of 84.8% (+2.2%) and a FNIR of 30.81% (-3.08%) on MEVID' - but Table 5 shows these exact numbers (84.8 Rank-1, 30.81 FNIR) belong to the CCVID row, not MEVID (MEVID's actual +Ours numbers are 55.1 Rank-1 and 64.80 FNIR). This is a direct mismatch between the paper's own prose and its own table, not just an interpretation issue.

Reported gains are inconsistent and sometimes negligible: GaitBase+Ours on GREW shows literally no closed-set improvement (60.1 -> 60.1 Rank@1) despite text describing the approach as consistently improving both closed- and open-set performance across the board.

The core hyperparameters (alpha, beta, gamma, lambda) are tuned via ablation on a single dataset/backbone combination (Gait3D with GaitBase, Table 2) and then reused as-is when applying the method to face recognition, a different gait backbone (SwinGait-3D), and person ReID - there's no shown re-tuning or sensitivity check confirming these hyperparameters transfer well across modalities.

A statistical significance test (two-sample t-test, p=0.052%) is reported for exactly one comparison (CAL vs +Ours on CCVID) out of the many comparisons made across three modalities and multiple datasets - the other, often smaller, margins (e.g. the MEVID or GREW results) get no significance testing despite being the kind of small deltas where it matters most.

Even after the proposed improvement, absolute open-set performance remains poor in practical terms - FNIR@1%FPIR stays above 60% on MEVID and above 75-80% on both gait datasets - meaning the majority of open-set probes are still mishandled; the paper's framing emphasizes the relative reduction rather than this remaining absolute gap.
notable: The train/test asymmetry pattern recurs across this literature review: like the earlier BMVC2023 SANet paper (Gumbel-Softmax at train time, hard argmax at test time), this paper uses differentiable sigmoid/softrank relaxations of detection and rank only during training, then falls back to the actual non-differentiable FNIR@FPIR computation at test time - a common and reusable trick for training toward metrics that aren't differentiable themselves. Also notable: the method is explicitly loss-only and modality-agnostic (bolted onto AdaFace/GaitBase/SwinGait/CAL unchanged), which is a nice generality argument, though it also means all reported gains are entirely attributable to training signal rather than any architectural insight specific to open-set biometrics.
